item.title: Hegseth, Pentagon officials reportedly floated using wartime law to reappoint Nvidia CEO
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
As senior members of the Trump administration huddled to discuss the embattled AI company Nvidia over the weekend, Pentagon leaders weighed an audacious idea: invoking a Cold War-era law to pressure Nvidia to restore Jensen Huang as CEO, according to three people familiar with the debate. The Defense Production Act, a 1950 law that grants the president broad authority to intervene in the economy, has historically been used to mobilize private companies to supply the military in wartime or during national emergencies. The first Trump administration used the law to prompt General Motors to produce ventilators during the covid-19 pandemic. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Before Huang’s return to Nvidia was announced Monday, Pentagon officials including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his senior deputy, Steve Feinberg, discussed how the DPA could be used as leverage to pressure Nvidia’s board to restore an executive to a company that they argued was critical to the national security of the United States, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive talks. While the law provides no clear path to installing a new CEO, it could be used as a warning. “Essentially they could use the DPA to force Nvidia to shift more of its production to military projects,” said one of the three people, a Trump administration official. That could have curbed the chipmaker’s production plans and profit. The conversation about the law as part of a campaign to place Huang back in power, which has not been previously reported, reflects the intensity with which the military views the AI race with China and the lengths the Trump administration may be willing to go to intervene in the economy. It also reveals another dimension of the Defense Department’s growing entanglement with Silicon Valley: Though the DPA has never been used to install a leader in a private company, the idea has gained currency with some influential members of the tech sector in recent weeks. It is unclear what was ultimately conveyed to Nvidia, or whether those arguments made their way to President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, both of whom ultimately became convinced that Huang needed to be back in his job. The two were willing to use the powerful muscle of the federal government to make that happen, as part of a “full-court press” by Cabinet officials over the weekend, one of the people said. Hegseth and Feinberg were part of that campaign, according to two of the people. Government officials emphasized during the talks that restoring Huang was important for U.S. national security, but Nvidia’s board did not perceive it as a threat, according to a person familiar with the board’s thinking. The president and vice president came to believe in the importance of Nvidia to the economy and its leader’s singular ability to stabilize financial markets, said two other people familiar with the discussions, who spoke on the condition of anonymity in order to describe them. Trump personally asked Vance to become involved in brokering the restoration of the embattled CEO as the scandal dragged down the stock market. Huang returned to Nvidia on Monday morning. The White House referred questions about the strategy to the Pentagon. “The conversations described between DOW senior leaders never happened and no such proposal was made by the Secretary, Deputy Secretary, or Under Secretary,” said a Pentagon official who refused to be named. (“DOW” refers to the Department of War, the administration’s preferred name for the Defense Department.) Nvidia spokesman Patrick Rutherford declined to comment. Under Hegseth, the Pentagon has made the development of AI capabilities a pillar of military strategy. In a memo issued early this year, he called for the military to become an “AI-first warfighting force” and said that “AI-enabled warfare and AI-enabled capability development will redefine the character of military affairs over the next decade.” Countries are racing to build such capabilities, under the belief that the nation with the fastest data processing power and the best models will become superior in future conflicts. Hegseth has entrusted the modernization of the military to Emil Michael, a seasoned Silicon Valley operator and former Uber executive who serves as undersecretary of defense for research and engineering and the military’s chief technology officer, and Feinberg, a billionaire who co-founded the private equity firm Cerberus Capital Management and is the No. 2 in the department. Together they have brought the military closer to the Silicon Valley companies Anduril and Palantir and to a growing number of start-ups and businesses in fields such as AI, quantum computing and critical minerals by giving out loans and in some cases investing directly in companies. Michael was also part of the conversations about DPA within the department, two of the people said. Pete Harrell, an attorney and visiting scholar at Georgetown’s Institute of International Economic Law, said it is unclear how the Defense Production Act could be used to reinstate Huang as chief executive of Nvidia but it raises alarms about how the Trump administration believes it can inject itself into the affairs of private corporations. “It’s not really interested in setting out … regulations,” he said. “It’s interested in getting five companies in a room and kind of telling them what to do.” The authority of the DPA is to basically put orders for the U.S. government ahead of anybody else, said Bill Greenwalt, a senior fellow and expert on the Defense Production Act at the American Enterprise Institute. Trying to suggest that the DPA could be leveraged to tie up Nvidia in government contracts isn’t supported at all in the act, Greenwalt said. A more effective way the administration could have pressured Nvidia without using the DPA would have been through export controls, he added. After Huang left, the idea of using the DPA to restore him gained currency in Silicon Valley circles. Last week the cryptocurrency investor Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at the firm Andreessen Horowitz, posted on social media that if the Nvidia board didn’t immediately restore Huang as CEO, “there’s actually a scenario where the Department of War steps in on Jensen’s side. Why? Given the likely cyberattacks on Microsoft, flights, banks, and now NSA, it’s arguably a matter of US national security to immediately return the most important person in AI to his role at the top AI company. Defense Production Act, but for the restoration of Jensen Huang.” Shervin Pishevar, a tech investor who worked with Michael at Uber, on Tuesday posted a long thread on X about the restoration of Huang, citing historical applications to argue that the Defense Production Act, if “properly applied, offers an important existing framework for strengthening America’s industrial base.” “Now that Jensen Huang is back, we should recognize that NVIDIA and America’s leadership in artificial intelligence are not simply matters of corporate governance or shareholder value,” he wrote. “They are matters of national security, economic competitiveness, and geopolitical power.” Pranshu Verma contributed to this report. Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/25/hegseth-pentagon-officials-floated-using-wartime-law-reappoint-nvidia-ceo/

item.title: Israel ramps up strikes on Hamas leaders in Gaza despite U.S. ceasefire pressure
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The damaged apartment block where Khaled Abu Nada, deputy minister of education in Gaza, was killed in an Israeli attack in Deir al-Balah, Gaza, on Thursday. - Moiz Salhi/Anadolu/Getty Images Israel has intensified its campaign of targeted assassinations in Gaza, striking and killing Hamas commanders and political leaders, as the Trump administration urges Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to proceed with the US-brokered ceasefire plan. On Thursday, the Israeli military killed Khaled Abu Nada, a senior member of Hamas’ Political Bureau and the organization’s Deputy Minister of Education, in a strike in central Gaza. According to a statement from Hamas, the strike on his residential apartment also killed his wife. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the killing of Abu Nada would disrupt Hamas’ “financial operations and its ability to formulate economic policy.” Hamas said the attack was the result of Israel’s “policy of systematic assassinations” and warned that “targeting civilian homes constitutes a continuous breach of the ceasefire agreement in Gaza and a flagrant violation of all international and humanitarian laws, norms, and conventions.” Since the nominal ceasefire was signed more than a year ago, Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza to target Hamas. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in Israeli strikes or military operations over that period. In recent weeks, Israel has escalated those strikes. On Wednesday, Israel struck and killed Muhammad Abu al-Aouf, the head of Hamas’ internal security apparatus in northern Gaza. A day earlier, the IDF killed al-Aouf’s commander, Naeem Muhammad Abu Nahal, who led Hamas’ internal security across Gaza. In each of these cases, the IDF said the assassination was a “blow” to Hamas’ leadership capabilities, even as the militant organization has firmly entrenched its power in the half of Gaza not occupied by the Israeli military. Mourners carry the bodies of Muhammad Abu al-Aouf, a Hamas internal security officer, and his family, killed in an Israeli strike according to the Hamas-run Health Minister, during their funeral in Gaza City, on Wednesday. - Jehad Alshrafi/AP The previous week, the IDF carried out strikes nearly every day targeting Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, from platoon leaders to commanders of Nukhba, a special force within Hamas’ military wing. In each case, the IDF issued virtually the same justification: “Throughout the war, and particularly recently, the terrorists advanced attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians and operated to restore the capabilities of terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip, in systematic violation of the ceasefire.” Hamas blamed both Israel and the US-backed Board of Peace for the ongoing attacks. The group said the board “bears political and moral responsibility for the continuation of these crimes as a result of its silence and failure to halt the aggression, and its continued provision of cover and support to the occupation.” The board was established by the Trump administration and backed by a UN Security Council resolution to advance the Gaza ceasefire plan signed in October 2025. But the plan stalled within weeks of its implementation, and much of Gaza remains in ruins. Globally isolated On Tuesday, Netanyahu spoke by phone with Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, who played a crucial role in crafting the ceasefire deal, according to an Israeli source who said they discussed Gaza. According to Axios , Kushner urged Netanyahu to carry out Israel’s obligations under the ceasefire plan, which would require Israel to stop striking Gaza and begin withdrawing forces that occupy more than half of the enclave’s territory. But Netanyahu has refused to make progress on the 20-point plan until Hamas is completely disarmed. Last week, Defense Minister Israel Katz said that Israel “will not withdraw from the current lines of the security zones” until Hamas is “dismantled.” He also warned that Israel is ready to occupy more of Gaza. Hamas has refused to unilaterally disarm, saying that it would only do so alongside a staged Israeli withdrawal from Gaza In an extensive interview with New York magazine , Kushner warned that Israel was increasingly becoming globally isolated. “I feel like the fork in the road is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, (and) be much more secure and much more integrated in the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global pariah status,” he said. In another interview, with Mathias Döpfner , CEO of POLITICO’s parent company Axel Springer, Kushner called Netanyahu someone who “doesn’t always make it easy” to make progress in the Trump administration’s Gaza plan, and delivered his sharpest rebuke of Israel’s broader posture, arguing it should drop its “constant wartime mindset” and embrace economic diplomacy like Gulf Arab states do. But Netanyahu has not shown any willingness to make concessions toward Gaza to advance the ceasefire agreement, particularly as his far-right allies have advocated for more strikes in Gaza and Palestinian emigration from the shattered territory. On Wednesday, Kushner said in a podcast interview that Israel “needs to get out of the constant wartime mindset and focus on economic diplomacy.” CNN’s Tal Shalev contributed to this article. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/26/middleeast/israel-gaza-assassinations-intl

item.title: Top official admits changes to federal wildfire response will result in 'deaths'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The senior official overseeing the U.S. Forest Service privately acknowledged this month that the Trump administration's urgent push to rapidly reshape how the nation responds to wildfires will lead to some wrong decisions that could cost lives, but suggested that it was necessary to learn from those to move forward with the task. "We're going to have to make decisions, some of which will be wrong. And some of those wrong decisions will lead to catastrophe," Michael Boren, the undersecretary of agriculture for national resources and development, said at an industry conference in San Francisco. "That'll lead to big costs, big disruption in people's lives and deaths. And we're going to have to recover from those and not let that debilitate us." Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. In a private session Nov. 4, Boren explained to about 100 attendees the challenges of unifying a "poor setup" of agencies into one force. He revealed the aggressive timeline, which has not been made public, that Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and President Donald Trump demanded: "We have limited information, severely limited time, because the Secretary wants us to be done with this in five months," he said. "And President Trump wants it done quicker than that." The Washington Post obtained a transcript of Boren's remarks at the Red Sky Summit, an annual conference that brings together high-profile leaders and technology innovators to solve the worsening wildfire crisis. Three Red Sky attendees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution, said Boren's comments are an important and rare acknowledgment from a top administration official that there have been significant costs from this year's restructuring of U.S. wildland firefighting, and it has taken a significant toll on the community. This has been a particularly deadly season for wildland firefighters across the United States. This year, 21 people have died, according to data from the Lessons Learned Center, a federal organization that tracks wildland fire safety. It has been the third deadliest year for the workforce since at least 2016, according to a Post review of two federal datasets. And while battling a record number of acres burned, fueled by dry wildlands and historically low snowpack, federal firefighters have also been navigating a massive reorganization in real time. For decades, firefighters have been spread across a few land management agencies, with the U.S. Forest Service overseeing the bulk of the country's firefighting force. The system has long struggled with retention issues, pay concerns, and organizational red tape. In January, the Trump administration established the U.S. Wildland Fire Service, whose mission is to streamline wildfire response and separate firefighters from land management oversight. Key elements of the reorganization await further study and congressional approval. As a result, departments that were already short-staffed as a result of the Department of Government Efficiency's campaign to slash the federal workforce have been trying to integrate while actively fighting fires. In absorbing this year's deaths, firefighters, experts and grieving family members have raised questions and concerns about efforts to reshape how the U.S. responds to fire, including opting for more aggressive tactics. In a statement to The Post for this report, Boren said that "the loss of even one life to wildfire is one too many, and protecting the lives of our firefighters and the American people is our highest priority." "My remarks at the Red Sky Summit were about our responsibility to learn from loss and continually improve our nation's wildfire prevention and response efforts," he said. "The Forest Service owes nothing less to the brave men and women who put their lives on the line to protect our communities." It is not clear exactly what Boren's five-month timeline referred to, since the process has been ongoing for longer than that. The USDA did not clarify when asked. This reorganization was a key topic of discussion at Red Sky this year. At the summit, Boren joined the director of the Wildland Fire Service, Brian Fennessy, and the Federal Emergency Management Administration's former U.S. fire administrator, Lori Moore-Merrell, for a conversation about the shifting architecture of the country's wildfire response, its challenges and why they think this change is necessary. In that initial conversationthey explained that under the new system, fire leaders, no longer those in charge of the land, will have the authority over major decisions such as prescribed burning projects and how fast to put out a fire. "We want the land managers at the table to tell us what those values at risk are from a resource perspective," Fennessy said, according to the public recording. "But when it comes to fighting fire and how we're doing that, we have the final say and we are the subject matter experts." They also shared their views on the controversial "full suppression" policy - a strategy the Trump administration has embraced that aims to attack fires to put them out as quickly as possible. "Full suppression isn't put out all fires," Boren countered. Instead, he said his approach is if a fire was not set intentionally to reduce fuels and the time of year is off, "we put it out." Boren, whom attendees described as soft-spoken, talked openly about what it's been like to overhaul the entire system. "Things are going well, even though they don't necessarily look like it on the surface," he told the crowd. "It's been very difficult for us to accomplish what we wanted to; we haven't been able to unify the agencies completely." After their 30-minute panel wrapped up, attendees were invited to stay to hear more in a private setting. That's when Boren spoke about having to conduct such a significant reorganization in "severely limited time," and what that could lead to. Red Sky offers "unconference conversations," according to its promotional materials, where attendees may ask leaders questions and have "frank" discussions. There is an understanding that the environment falls under the Chatham House Rule, attendees said, where participants can describe the substance of what is discussed but not who said what. Boren made these remarks during one of these settings. The Post obtained a transcript from the smaller session and independently verified Boren's remarks with conference attendees. One attendee, who has spent decades in land management, fire science and response, said Boren's comments struck a nerve, and they questioned "the casual acceptance that firefighter deaths are a necessary price of engaging with wildland fire." Riva Duncan, president of Grassroots Wildland Firefighters and a former U.S. Forest Service official, had also heard about the comments earlier this month. And while her group has advocated for a unified fire service, she said "to hear a top official prioritize an arbitrary and ridiculous timeline, and knowingly make bad decisions, over people's lives is unconscionable." She added, "Establishing a unified wildfire service intentionally and mindfully should take time, and no one, not wildland firefighters nor citizens, should have to pay for that with their lives." Bill Clerico, the founder of Red Sky, said the summit gathers about 600 leaders "who take time out of their busy schedules to discuss, debate and collaborate on difficult issues. Many of the conversations, including the off-the-record session referenced, grappled with the need for systems reform and the challenges posed by transition." Boren, who is a rancher and tech executive, has been a contentious figure. He owns thousands of acres in Idaho, including a 480-acre ranch within the Sawtooth National Recreation Area, and has had conflicts with the Forest Service, which he now oversees, largely about his use of those federal lands in Idaho. This summer, he asked Forest Service staff to escalate its response to a small fire near his property, which pulled aircraft off other fires. At the time, Agriculture Department spokesman Michael Abboud said that Boren did call officials about the fire, but "at no point did he pressure leadership or order more resources to fight this or any other fire." During their public panel at the conference, Boren and Fennessy discussed the red tape surrounding U.S. fire response, and how it has thwarted necessary work such as intentionally setting controlled fires to avert larger blazes. Boren described a culture among federal agencies to "want to do their own thing," and said that "we need to be a unified service that provides consistent service to the American people across the entire nation." While it has been challenging, Boren said, he thinks having a single fire service in charge of fire decisions is the best move for the country. Boren told the crowd there were two reasons he came to government: "One of them - I won't talk about the other today 'cause [it's a] different Forest Service topic - one of the two primary reasons is I felt that the way we handled fires was really foolish and it comes down to this problem: Who's in charge when there's a fire?" As moderator, Moore-Merrell asked officials about the loss of life this year, specifically citing the deaths of four firefighters in Colorado, a tragedy that spurred concern and outrage over the direction of U.S. firefighting. "These are great, interesting jobs. Young people want to have these jobs and they're glad to have them," Boren said. "And it's really important for us to make sure that we appropriately reduce the risk to them." That is one of the main reasons to unify, he said, to "maximize safety" by putting firefighters "in a position where they have much more control over what they're doing and much more information about what's going on around them." During the subsequent private discussion, Boren continued to speak candidly about spearheading this massive systematic change. "The crux of the whole issue is land management versus fire," he said, according to the transcript reviewed by The Post. The problems, he said, came from a "poor setup of the agencies and of the incentives within the agencies," such as money, budgets and decisions about who gets what resources. Some in the audience told The Post the remark about how wrong decisions could lead to deaths gave them pause. One attendee said that although Boren did not say it "brazenly," it was a sobering acknowledgment, this person said, of the grave consequence in all this: People will die. Another attendee said they were put off by how "he moved from an administrative deadline to potentially fatal consequences without mentioning the lives lost this year or any empathy for them, and no mention of safeguards they might put in place to prevent those consequences." A third attendee, an expert in wildland fire policy who was at both events, did not immediately recall hearing Boren's comment. But when read the transcript, they had a "visceral" reaction to it. This person said that Boren's comments highlighted the administration's approach of treating firefighting like combat, where there is a "number of deaths they expect to occur." "If we were in the military I would say that's part of the expectation of fighting a war, that people will die," the expert said. "But we hire young people to do this work of land and resource management. They don't sign up for protecting life and property believing they may in fact be the ones who will die." Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/climate-environment/2026/11/26/top-us-official-says-wrong-decisions-deaths-expected-wildfire-shake-up/

item.title: Trump calls earlier GDP figures 'fake' after growth is revised from 3.4% to 4.3%
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday accused his Commerce Department of purposely issuing incorrect economic growth figures before the midterm elections, and said he wants to launch an investigation. Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine trust in economic data that fails to match his claims of a historic boom, a pattern that threatens the credibility of figures needed by businesses, financial markets and consumers when making investments. His latest complaint concerns data issued by the Commerce Department on Wednesday that revised gross domestic product in the third quarter to 4.3% on an annual basis, up from a prior estimate of 3.4%. The department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis routinely updates its economic data to improve their accuracy. GDP figures, monthly jobs reports and other data are regularly revised. Those updates occur on a pre-scheduled basis without regard to the political calendar. But the president claimed on social media that it was a “massive, and purposeful, error” and linked it to the poor performance for Republicans in the Nov. 3 midterm elections that gave Democrats control of both houses of Congress. “It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE, and a correction was issued yesterday by the people in the Government Agency that does these numbers,” Trump posted. “Why wasn't the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation.” The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The government is largely closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday. It’s the latest instance of Trump questioning the integrity of economic data he feels is unfavorable to him without providing evidence that revisions are politically motivated. In August 2025, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics after a decidedly weak jobs report. That report said only 73,000 jobs were added in July 2025 and showed that 258,000 fewer jobs were added in May and June than previously reported. Trump called that jobs report “phony” and “rigged.” Trump has claimed that he deserves credit for powering stronger economic growth, but voters do not share the president's belief that the economy is strong. In the midterms, 76% described economic conditions as “not so good” or “poor,” according to the AP Voter Poll, an extensive survey of the electorate. About two-thirds of voters said Trump’s own policies had fueled inflation. The president in his social media post ignored that the same federal agency on Wednesday also reported that a key measure of inflation — the personal consumption expenditures price index — accelerated to an annual pace of 3.8% in October. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-calls-gdp-figures-fake-160813047.html

item.title: Oil prices climb as Iran reports 2 tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Amanda Stephenson CALGARY, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Crude oil prices rose on Thursday after Yemen's Houthis said they hit Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery, and Iran said mines struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz, ‌reviving concerns about supply disruptions. Brent crude futures settled at $96.57 a barrel, up $1.96, or 1.2%. US West Texas ‌Intermediate crude futures, which did not settle on Thursday because of the US Thanksgiving holiday, were up $1.16, or 1.39%, at $84.84 as of 1:21 ​p.m. ET (1821 GMT). A series of events this week increased geopolitical worries and the Middle East risk premium. On Wednesday, the Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, part of a complex that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude. At the same time, shipping has been disrupted through the Strait of Hormuz, where oil ‌supply had been recovering to levels close ⁠to those before the Iran war. On Thursday, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers had exploded and caught fire after hitting sea mines north of Oman's Khasab port while attempting ⁠to cross the strait. One of the vessels was a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, the Guards said. "This is keeping the market on edge into the (Thanksgiving) holiday," said Phil Flynn, senior analyst at Price Futures Group. While data will ​probably ​show a small global supply surplus in October, said Commodity ​Context founder Rory Johnston, the outlook for crude ‌prices is bullish. He cited slowing Hormuz flows, low inventories, and what he called "known, acute risk" to approximately 15% of global supplies. "My view is that we were oversold when (Brent) was dipping below $90," Johnston said. "It was only a matter of time before we tightened again." SPOTLIGHT MOVES TO OPEC+ OPEC+ ministers will hold meetings on Sunday to decide their 2027 output policy. They face the challenge of balancing output with the United Arab Emirates no longer in the group, and ‌with Iraq and Kazakhstan pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate ​of their oil production capacity. Two people with knowledge of the matter said OPEC+ ​may roll over its current oil output targets ​at the meeting for at least the first quarter of 2027. US crude stocks rose by ‌1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in ​the week ended November 20, ​the Energy Information Administration said. That supported prices because analysts had expected a rise of 1.5 million barrels. [EIA/S] In Asia, Thailand's Bangchak Corp said it had shut all production units at its Phra Khanong oil refinery in ​Bangkok after a fire. A drone attack ‌at the Slavyansk ECO oil refinery in Russia's southern Krasnodar region also led to a fire, ​inflicting serious damage. (Reporting by Amanda Stephenson in Calgary, Seher Dareen in London and Sudarshan Varadhan in ​Singapore; Editing by Bill Berkrot, Rod Nickel and Chris Reese) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/oil-rises-supply-concerns-iran-030849858.html

item.title: Scott, Thune headed for clash over permanent daylight saving time
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), one of President Trump’s closest Senate allies, is girding for a clash with Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) over a House-passed bill to make daylight saving time permanent. Scott said he will insist on getting a vote on the Sunshine Protection Act, which has strong support from Trump, before Christmas even though Thune has signaled he’s not a fan of the bill and other Republicans, including Sen. Tom Cotton (Ark.), have vowed to oppose it. “Tom Cotton’s against it,” Scott acknowledged but insisted that won’t stop the bill from getting a vote on the Senate floor. “It’s going to come up for a vote.” Black Friday-Cyber Monday Deals Black Friday cell phone and accessories deals Black Friday home deals: Up to 60% off bedding, smart home and more Black Friday deals perfect for stocking stuffers BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission. The Florida senator said he doesn’t have any assurance from Thune on that, but he’s intent on making that happen. “I’m going to do whatever it takes to get a vote,” Scott vowed. “I’m OK with people voting against it. I’m going to get a vote.” Scott has pressed for action on the bill for months. But now he has the leverage he needs to force the issue to the floor, as Thune will need cooperation from his entire conference to speed up floor procedures to consider as many of his legislative priorities as possible before Democrats seize control of the upper chamber in January. Thune told Semafor in an interview that Trump is constantly pressing him to act on the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time year-round across the country. The version of the bill marked up in the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee has a two-year implementation delay that would give states a chance to opt out of permanent daylight saving time. Thune said Trump has called him “I don’t know how many times on it.” The legislation passed the House in July by a vote of 308 to 117. Thune says the proposal is not popular in northern Plains states such as South Dakota because if enacted it would result in late sunrise times during the winter. “Sunrise in Pierre would be like 9:25 in the morning. It’s a Northern Plains type issue, and that’s a lot of Republican senators. It’s Montana, Idaho, Nebraska, Iowa, South and North Dakota,” Thune told Semafor. Thune told Politico in an interview last month that there’s “no clear path forward or consensus” on moving the Sunshine Protection Act in the lame-duck session. But the legislation could get strong support from Democrats, such as Sens. Ed Markey (Mass.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), who backed it when it passed the Senate by unanimous consent in 2022. Markey says “more sun means more fun,” and Whitehouse has argued that studies show economic activity is reduced during standard time while permanent daylight saving time would result in “greater energy savings.” Thune may have a tough time rebuffing Scott’s demand for a vote if Trump insists that he be heard. Trump criticized the Senate for failing to act on the proposal after the nation set the clock back an hour earlier this month. “Too bad the Senate has not yet approved the Sunshine Protection Act or, the ‘I Don’t Want to Change My Clocks Anymore Act,'” the president posted on Truth Social . “It’s so dark outside, so early (Sunset was 5:06 P.M., and it was dark by 5:31 P.M. — Isn’t that ridiculous?). Just a few days ago it was so nice and sunny at this same time,” he wrote. Cotton, the chair of the Senate Republican Conference, is the leading opponent to the legislation, and GOP colleagues expect him to wage a filibuster to block it on the floor. That means it could take up to a week of valuable floor time to schedule votes on the legislation, time that Thune doesn’t want to spend on a bill that he doesn’t embrace. The Senate is scheduled to be in session three more weeks in December before departing town for the Christmas and New Year’s recess. Thune noted to reporters earlier this year that he opposed the legislation when it was considered in the Commerce Committee. Support for the legislation largely breaks along regional lines depending on how permanent daylight saving time would affect the times of sunrise and sunset in various states. The sun would rise as late as 9:30 a.m. in parts of Montana, North Dakota and Michigan’s Upper Peninsula during the depths of winter; and parts of the country, including Indiana, North Dakota, Oregon and Texas, would see more than 100 days of winter with sunrises after 8 a.m. But Southern and coastal states such as Florida, Georgia, Alabama, South Carolina and parts of Texas, which have mild winters, could benefit from increased tourism and outdoor recreation during the winter if daylight saving time were made year-round. “It’s probably the most popular thing I passed as governor,” said Scott, who signed a state law to make daylight saving time year-round in 2018. The bill was contingent on federal approval, however. Cotton argues Congress made daylight saving time permanent in 1973 but then quickly reversed course after lawmakers realized the “second-order implications of the change.” “You can simply learn the lesson of history. Congress did this once before,” he said, noting that polling showed 79 percent of Americans favored making daylight saving time year-round in 1973. But support for the idea plummeted to 42 percent in 1974 after Congress made the change. “People had experienced daylight savings time in the depth of winter. item.title: Gérard Depardieu will stand trial in rape case after French actor loses appeal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Gérard Depardieu will stand trial in a criminal court on a rape charge related to accusations by actress Charlotte Arnould, after an appeal by his lawyers failed. The Paris Court of Appeal said on Thursday that Depardieu would be tried for one part of the accusations levelled by Arnould against the actor. More from Deadline Gérard Depardieu Drops Appeal Against Sexual Assault Verdict & Acknowledges Guilt In Statement Titled 'I Hear' French Actor Gérard Depardieu To Face Rape Trial In Criminal Court Juliette Binoche On Gérard Depardieu's Guilty Sexual Assault Verdict: "He's Not A Sacred Monster, He's A Man Who Lost His Aura" - Cannes The actress, whose father was an old friend of the actor, accuses Depardieu of raping and sexually assaulting her twice in his Paris mansion in the summer of 2018 after she went to him for acting advice. The court has ruled that Depardieu will be tried for the first alleged rape on August 7, 2018, but not the second alleged rape on August 13, due to insufficient evidence. The decision to proceed with the trail comes eight months after Depardieu was found guilty of sexual assault and given an 18-month suspended sentence related to events on the set of Jean Becker’s The Green Shutters in 2021. The acto r last week announced he was abandoning plans to appeal the sentence and issued a statement saying that he recognized his culpability and apologized for the hurt he had caused. Just days after the letter was published, investigative newsite Mediapart published details of a fresh sexual assault and rape complaint against the actor related to events on the shoot of Guillaume Nicloux’s Thalasso in 2018. His 18-month suspended sentence related to assaults on two female crew members on the set of The Green Shutters . A number of women, who were not pressing charges, also gave evidence at the trial, including an actress who alleged Depardieu had shoved his hands into her knickers during a photo-call on the set of Netflix show Marseille . Arnould was the first woman to pursue Depardieu in the courts in relation to sexual assault allegations, but her move came against a backdrop of growing rumors around the actor’s sexually inappropriate treatment of female extras and crew members on film sets. Her complaint was initially dismissed by the courts following a nine-month investigation for lack of evidence, but she filed a second complaint as a civil party, which resulted in an investigating judge being appointed in 2020, and Depardieu being indicted for rape and sexual assault in 2021. In between times, Depardieu’s public star plummeted following an exposé of his alleged sexual misconduct by state broadcaster channel France 2’s investigative show Complément d’Enquête , entitled “The fall of the ogre”, which aired in December 2023. The allegations and 2026 guilty verdict have brought his acting career to a grinding halt. Since 2022, he has worked on only three productions, one of them directed by his longtime friend Fanny Ardant. The criminal court is France’s highest level of court reserved for crimes carrying sentences of more than five years, if the accused is found guilty.
